extracted.intended_audience: academic referees and authors in computer science and mathematics (journal reviewers, graduate students learning to referee)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for referees (peer reviewers) on evaluating journal submissions and for authors on presenting papers and illustrations in mathematics/computer-science publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper outcome categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperl generally will fall into the following categories: 1. Publish essentially as is; the only changes necessary are very simple typographical matter. 2. Publish after author's minor revision; the referee indicates points pertinent to the standards for publication which must be changed before the paper is published. 3. Publish only if the author makes major revisions. 4. Reject (there is nothing salvageable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to give an overall recommendation. When rejecting, the referee is asked to suggest a less prestigious journal that might publish such work (a downward-filtering practice described here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of a referee
rubrics_metrics.description: The goals of a referee are to keep the quality of publication as high as possible and also to help the author to produce a better paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reports to give the author maximum benefit while not compromising on quality. Aim to improve the work (point out errors, suggest literature, suggest exposition improvements) rather than merely gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution / significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should contribute to the state of the art; if it is purely expository it should be clearly designated as a good expository paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the paper makes a genuine contribution or whether it's mainly exposition. If contribution is marginal but salvageable via rewriting, recommend major revision rather than outright rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: All technical material must be correct (e.g., no incorrect equations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for subtle technical errors; when in doubt authors sometimes must be asked to verify (e.g., by writing a program). Point out incorrect equations, invalid arguments, or gaps in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to earlier work / literature adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should check that the paper makes adequate reference to earlier work in the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide missing references when possible. Lack of adequate citation is a common shortcoming, especially when the author ventures into an unfamiliar field.

rubrics_metrics.name: English style and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: English style — The article must be identifiable, readable, solidly written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on readability, clarity, and presentation; point out misleading phrasing or overly subtle exposition. Suggest notation changes and typographical fixes to improve comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The bibliography should be adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure citations are complete and appropriate for situating the work; suggest additional key references when missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee report format and submission practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Return the manuscript to the editor; please don't mark it up. Submit the report in duplicate, either of which one copy will be sent directly to the author; you may also write an accompanying letter to the editor or the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow journal procedures: don't annotate the author's copy, prepare a clean report (duplicate if requested), and consider an accompanying letter to the editor if you wish (which should not be passed on to the author if specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn it in immediately (don't postpone). Remember that the referee cycle is the critical path toward publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return reports promptly (e.g., within requested four weeks). Delays slow publication for many authors and can make timely checks impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical checks (typographical, notation, presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should note typographic errors, suggest notation changes, and point out where presentation is misleading or overly subtle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small fixes (typos, notation clarifications) are valuable; indicate which issues are cosmetic versus which affect correctness or comprehension. Suggest concrete rewordings or notation improvements when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing references and pointers
rubrics_metrics.description: Good referees supply a slew of references to other work and can point out references the author could not have found easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing missed but relevant literature and suggesting further reading can materially improve the author's paper and inspire new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid and identify 'facile generalizations' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facile generalizations — generalizations that are merely mechanical manipulations of a given argument without creating new insight — are not helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call out when authors produce superficial generalizations and advise whether such material adds value or should be omitted/refocused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of checklists or specific questions for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking referees to answer a specific list of questions might cause a referee to consider issues he might otherwise have forgotten about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to explicit editorial questions carefully; use them to structure your report and ensure you cover significance, correctness, exposition, related work, and suitability for the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity, conflicts, and ethical behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The identities of referees are usually hidden from the author; occasionally the identity of the author is hidden from referees (blind review). Referees sometimes make substantive improvements while anonymous; anonymity also allows a referee to publish competing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of conflicts of interest. Use anonymity responsibly: provide credit in acknowledgements where appropriate, avoid exploiting privileged knowledge to compete unfairly, and follow the journal's conflict rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment about requesting major rewrites vs rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper is a candidate significant enough to warrant additional amount of labor to rewrite and resubmit, consider asking for a rewrite rather than rejecting outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the paper's underlying contribution when deciding between recommending major revision and recommending rejection; give the author a chance to improve significant work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams — keep small and purposeful
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small; detailed diagrams can exist for those who want to see detail but should not overwhelm the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams to clarify opaque accounts; small, well-focused figures are preferable. If detail is included, make it optionally ignorable by the casual reader, and accompany diagrams with explanatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data for examples
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to use 'real' data than 'sample data' that have in fact been cooked up solely to use as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer genuine illustrative data (e.g., a paragraph from Grimm's Fairy Tales) to contrived examples; real data give a more meaningful demonstration of algorithmic or expository behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color use
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can be used effectively in talks, but usually not in papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve color for presentations; consider the journal's printing policy and cost—most printed papers are grayscale and should not rely on color to convey essential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of illustrations (production effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of work involved in preparing a paper for publication is proportional to the cube of the number of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be judicious in requesting many figures; each additional illustration increases production effort and cost for authors and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables and numerical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical tables can sometimes present ideas that can't be demonstrated graphically (e.g., numbers oscillating about 2 with period 211).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables when graphs are inadequate; ensure tables are clear and arranged so text referring to them appears close (e.g., opposite the diagrams they reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure placement and accompanying text
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange final text opposite the diagrams to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it easy for readers to find explanatory text for each figure; coordinate layout with the publisher/printer to avoid confusing separations between figure and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams for algorithmic exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams (graphs, ATNs, nested boxes) are useful to convey structure of algorithms and parsing; nested diagrams can replace more traditional trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the diagram type that best matches the conceptual structure (e.g., graphs for least-cost path, ATNs for parsing). Use diagrams to give readers a handle on complicated data structures or processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of misleading visualizations (ethical presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that visual choices can mislead (example from Huff/Tufte: choosing heights/volumes to exaggerate differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design figures to honestly represent relative magnitudes (avoid 3D/volume illusions that distort perception); follow good practice in quantitative graphics (scale choice, axes labeling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting and printer instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a printed example deliberately looks wrong (e.g., extreme line-stretching), tell the printers that this was deliberate to avoid 'correction'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag any deliberate typographic oddities to the production team so they are not 'corrected' during typesetting; communicate clearly about required figure reproduction (angles, fold-outs, color).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-writing and notation economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize subscripts and superscripts; avoid subscripted subscripts or subscripted superscripts. Hold back before enumerating elements; use words instead of heavy notation when clearer; factor proofs into subgoals and provide orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for perspicuity: simplify notation, prefer English words where they improve readability, break proofs into manageable pieces with clear interfaces, and tell the reader the proof strategy (e.g., 'essentially a diagonalization technique').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical summaries (histograms, scattergrams, tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Histograms and scattergrams can illustrate algorithmic behavior (e.g., distribution of distorted lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such summaries to support claims about performance or frequency; be transparent about biases (e.g., rewriting of particularly ugly paragraphs biases distortion statistics).
